Day 4. At a desk in the relief camp, Gopika filled in the forms for flood assistance while the clerk stamped each page. Her ID card and mark sheets had gone brown in the water, so she also listed them as lost.

Day 12. Thomas, the insurance agent from the bank, sat with her while she attached photos of the waterline on the walls and of the ruined books to the claim. She also wrote to the college for duplicate papers.

Day 30. Gopika had been waking at night, listening for water that was not there. She noticed it was not getting better on its own. On Monday she booked a weekly slot with the college counsellor and wrote it in the same notebook as her list of papers.

qa.q: What did Gopika attach to the insurance claim?
qa.a: She attached photos of the waterline on the walls and of the ruined books.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling on Day 30 when she woke at night?
qa.a: Gopika was frightened and worn down, realising that the nights were not getting better on their own.

qa.q: What else could help Gopika's recovery, and why?
qa.a: Gopika could keep a folder of every receipt and reply and lean on friends for the tiring parts, because recovery has many small steps and sharing them lightens the load.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Gopika's way of going about it?
qa.a: Thomas would probably feel that a claim with photos and forms in order is easier to process, and might feel some relief at working with someone so organised.

passage:
"Mohit, you asked how we got back on our feet after the flood. I, Harish, your old neighbour, will tell you straight: for the first month, we didn't.
I was twenty-one. The water took the ground floor, my certificates, the shop stock. I sat on the steps every day doing nothing but feeling heavy. Then one night I couldn't sleep and I thought, I'm waiting for everything to fix itself at once. It won't.
So I made stages on a sheet of paper. Week one: apply for the government relief at the ward office. Week two: the insurance claim, with the photos I'd luckily taken on my phone before cleaning. Week three: go to the college and the tehsil office to replace my lost papers, one by one.
And stage four, which I nearly skipped: talk to the counsellor at the relief camp. I thought that was for weak people. It wasn't. It was the stage that let me finish the others."

qa.q: What did Harish plan for week two?
qa.a: The insurance claim, with the photos taken on the phone before cleaning.

qa.q: How did Harish feel during the first month after the flood?
qa.a: Harish felt heavy and stuck, sitting on the steps every day doing nothing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Harish's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Realising on a sleepless night that nothing would fix itself at once was the turning point, because it led to breaking recovery into stages.

qa.q: How might the counsellor at the relief camp have seen Harish's visit?
qa.a: The counsellor likely saw someone carrying a lot of stress who was brave enough to come, even while thinking it was for weak people.

grounding: Shows a person after a flood applying for relief, filing an insurance claim with photos, replacing papers and speaking to a counsellor, in planned stages.

passage:
Three weeks after the cyclone, Nandini's phone was still at the repair shop and the only working computer was in the crowded panchayat office, open two hours a day. Her family's papers had been soaked. She had been crying at night and snapping at her sister Ishita in the day.
"We can't do everything at once," she said one morning, and wrote a list in stages on the back of a relief packet.
Stage one: the relief form at the panchayat office, queue at eight. Stage two: the insurance claim for the house, using photos Ishita had taken on her own phone. Stage three: new copies of the ration card and her marksheets, one office each week. Stage four: the counsellor who visited the camp on Thursdays.
The queue on Monday took four hours. She got the relief receipt. On Thursday she sat with the counsellor for half an hour and cried, and afterwards, for the first time, she slept through the night.

qa.q: Whose phone had the photos for the insurance claim?
How was Nandini feeling in the weeks after the cyclone, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was stressed and overwhelmed, crying at night and snapping at Ishita during the day.

qa.q: What else could Nandini do to keep the stages moving?
qa.a: She could share the list with Ishita so they split the offices, making each week's step lighter.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel as Nandini starts sleeping again?
qa.a: Ishita would likely feel relieved and closer to her sister, after days of being snapped at.

grounding: Shows a person after a disaster applying for relief, claiming insurance with photos, replacing papers and seeing a counsellor in planned stages.
